summary: Give the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator the yearly demand, the order cost and the yearly cost of holding and it returns economic order quantity (EOQ). It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator work?
sections.html:
The Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports economic order quantity (EOQ) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the yearly demand, the order cost and the yearly cost of holding.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Economic order quantity (EOQ)=the square root of (2) × the square root of (order cost × yearly demand ÷ yearly cost of holding)
Economic order quantity (EOQ)=eoq print

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Yearly demand = 10 units, Order cost = 10 and Yearly cost of holding = 10. The calculator returns Economic order quantity (EOQ) = 4.472 units and Eoq print = 4.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Economic order quantity (EOQ) = 4.472 units and Eoq print = 4 should be roughly the size you expected from Yearly demand = 10 units and Order cost = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in units/points (1), and convertible to any of the 9 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Quantity, opening in units/points (1)
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Quantity, opening in units/points (1)

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Preparing questions for a lender, an accountant or an adviser
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the yearly demand, the order cost and the yearly cost of holding — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns economic order quantity (EOQ), derived from the yearly demand, the order cost and the yearly cost of holding. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the yearly demand, the order cost and the yearly cost of holding, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter yearly demand in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Yearly demand opens in units/points (1) and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Economic order quantity (EOQ) = 4.472 units. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Economic order quantity (EOQ) calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
